claim: Metabolic co-regulation between biosynthetic pathways for secondary metabolites is common in microbes.
source: Metabolic co-regulation between biosynthetic pathways for secondary metabolites is common in microbes and can play an important role in microbial interactions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the broader scientific literature context.

claim: Metabolic co-regulation can play an important role in microbial interactions.
source: Metabolic co-regulation between biosynthetic pathways for secondary metabolites is common in microbes and can play an important role in microbial interactions.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the context of the study.

claim: An intermediate in DAPG biosynthesis, phloroglucinol, is transformed by a halogenase encoded in the pyoluteorin gene cluster into mono- and di-chlorinated phloroglucinols.
source: We show that an intermediate in DAPG biosynthesis, phloroglucinol, is transformed by a halogenase encoded in the pyoluteorin gene cluster into mono- and di-chlorinated phloroglucinols.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including LCMS analysis, in vitro enzyme assays, and genetic studies presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chlorinated phloroglucinols function as intra- and inter-cellular signals that induce the expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes.
source: The chlorinated phloroglucinols function as intra- and inter-cellular signals that induce the expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes, pyoluteorin production, and pyoluteorin-mediated inhibition of the plant-pathogenic bacterium Erwinia amylovora.
evidence: This is supported by GFP reporter assays, co-culture experiments, and antibiosis assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Chlorinated phloroglucinols induce pyoluteorin production.
source: The chlorinated phloroglucinols function as intra- and inter-cellular signals that induce the expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes, pyoluteorin production, and pyoluteorin-mediated inhibition of the plant-pathogenic bacterium Erwinia amylovora.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC quantification of pyoluteorin in cultures amended with chlorinated phloroglucinols.

claim: Chlorinated phloroglucinols induce pyoluteorin-mediated inhibition of Erwinia amylovora.
source: The chlorinated phloroglucinols function as intra- and inter-cellular signals that induce the expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes, pyoluteorin production, and pyoluteorin-mediated inhibition of the plant-pathogenic bacterium Erwinia amylovora.
evidence: This is supported by antibiosis assays showing inhibition of E. amylovora by co-cultures that produce pyoluteorin.

claim: This metabolic co-regulation provides a strategy for P. protegens to optimize the deployment of secondary metabolites with distinct roles in cooperative and competitive microbial interactions.
source: This metabolic co-regulation provides a strategy for P. protegens to optimize the deployment of secondary metabolites with distinct roles in cooperative and competitive microbial interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and ecological context.

claim: Many microorganisms produce multiple secondary metabolites with diverse chemical properties and ecological functions.
source: Many microorganisms produce multiple secondary metabolites with diverse chemical properties and ecological functions that contribute to the fitness of the producing organism in natural environments (Haas and Keel, 2003; O'Brien and Wright 2011, Traxler and Kolter, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The biosynthesis of different secondary metabolites by a microorganism is often coordinated.
source: The biosynthesis of different secondary metabolites by a microorganism is often coordinated (Bosello et al., 2011; Tsunematsu et al., 2013; Hidalgo et al., 2014; Vingadassalon et al., 2015; Cano-Prieto et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Co-regulation of different secondary metabolites is thought to be selected during microbial evolution because it confers competitive advantages to the producing organism in microbial interactions.
source: Co-regulation of different secondary metabolites is thought to be selected during microbial evolution because it confers competitive advantages to the producing organism in microbial interactions (Challis and Hopwood, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DAPG and pyoluteorin are two broad-spectrum antibiotics with toxicity against fungi, bacteria, oomycetes and plants.
source: This study focuses on 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG) and pyoluteorin, two broad-spectrum antibiotics with toxicity against fungi, bacteria, oomycetes and plants (Ohmori et al., 1978; Keel et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Certain strains of Pseudomonas spp. produce DAPG but not pyoluteorin.
source: Certain strains of Pseudomonas spp. produce DAPG but not pyoluteorin (Loper et al., 2012) and some strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa produce pyoluteorin but not DAPG (Ohmori et al., 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa produce pyoluteorin but not DAPG.
source: Certain strains of Pseudomonas spp. produce DAPG but not pyoluteorin (Loper et al., 2012) and some strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa produce pyoluteorin but not DAPG (Ohmori et al., 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only a subset of strains of the species Pseudomonas protegens are known to produce both DAPG and pyoluteorin.
source: To date, only a subset of strains of the species Pseudomonas protegens are known to produce both compounds (Loper et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: P. protegens Pf-5 produces both DAPG and pyoluteorin.
source: Among these DAPG- and pyoluteorin-producing strains is the soil bacterium P. protegens Pf-5.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: In the genome of Pf-5, genes for DAPG and pyoluteorin biosynthesis are present in two different gene clusters separated by 3.7-megabases.
source: In the genome of Pf-5, genes for DAPG and pyoluteorin biosynthesis are present in two different gene clusters (Figure 1A and C) separated by 3.7-megabases (Paulsen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the genome sequence and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The biosynthetic substrates and intermediates of the DAPG and pyoluteorin pathways are distinct.
source: The biosynthetic substrates and intermediates of the two pathways are distinct (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 showing the distinct biosynthetic pathways.

claim: DAPG biosynthesis begins with synthesis of phloroglucinol (PG) from three molecules of malonyl-CoA by the type III polyketide synthase PhlD.
source: DAPG biosynthesis begins with synthesis of phloroglucinol (PG) from three molecules of malonyl-CoA by the type III polyketide synthase PhlD (Achkar et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PG is acetylated through the action of PhlABC to form DAPG.
source: PG is then acetylated through the action of PhlABC to form DAPG (Bangera and Thomashow, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pyoluteorin biosynthesis begins with activation of L-proline by the L-prolyl-AMP ligase PltF, and attachment to the peptidyl-carrier protein PltL.
source: Pyoluteorin biosynthesis begins with activation of L-proline by the L-prolyl-AMP ligase PltF, and attachment to the peptidyl-carrier protein PltL (Thomas et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The Pro-S-PltL intermediate is oxidized by PltE and chlorinated by PltA to yield 4,5-dichloropyrrolyl-S-PltL.
source: The Pro-S-PltL intermediate is oxidized by PltE and chlorinated by PltA to yield 4,5-dichloropyrrolyl-S-PltL (Thomas et al., 2002; Dorrestein et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The dichloropyrrole is extended by the type I polyketide synthase PltBC followed by release and formation of the resorcinol, presumably catalyzed by PltG to yield pyoluteorin.
source: The dichloropyrrole is extended by the type I polyketide synthase PltBC followed by release and formation of the resorcinol, presumably catalyzed by PltG to yield pyoluteorin (Nowak-Thompson et al., 1997, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Production of DAPG and pyoluteorin by P. protegens is tightly coordinated.
source: Despite the independent biochemical and genetic determinants for their biosynthesis, production of DAPG and pyoluteorin by P. protegens is tightly coordinated.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutations in pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes result in loss of pyoluteorin production along with overproduction of DAPG.
source: Mutations in pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes result in loss of pyoluteorin production along with overproduction of DAPG (Brodhagen et al., 2004; Quecine et al., 2016), and addition of pyoluteorin to bacterial cultures represses the expression of certain DAPG biosynthetic genes and the production of DAPG (Schnider-Keel et al., 2000; Baehler et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Addition of pyoluteorin to bacterial cultures represses the expression of certain DAPG biosynthetic genes and the production of DAPG.
source: Mutations in pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes result in loss of pyoluteorin production along with overproduction of DAPG (Brodhagen et al., 2004; Quecine et al., 2016), and addition of pyoluteorin to bacterial cultures represses the expression of certain DAPG biosynthetic genes and the production of DAPG (Schnider-Keel et al., 2000; Baehler et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nanomolar concentrations of PG are required for pyoluteorin production.
source: Conversely, PG, an intermediate in DAPG biosynthesis, has a concentration-dependent influence on expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes and production of pyoluteorin: nanomolar concentrations of PG are required for pyoluteorin production but micromolar concentrations of PG repress pyoluteorin production (Kidarsa et al., 2011; Clifford et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Micromolar concentrations of PG repress pyoluteorin production.
source: Conversely, PG, an intermediate in DAPG biosynthesis, has a concentration-dependent influence on expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes and production of pyoluteorin: nanomolar concentrations of PG are required for pyoluteorin production but micromolar concentrations of PG repress pyoluteorin production (Kidarsa et al., 2011; Clifford et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A phlD mutant produces neither pyoluteorin nor DAPG.
source: The essential role of PG in pyoluteorin production became evident when we discovered that a phlD mutant, which lacks the type III polyketide synthase PhlD responsible for PG biosynthesis, produces neither pyoluteorin nor DAPG.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The phlD mutant can be complemented for pyoluteorin production by addition of nanomolar concentrations of PG to the culture medium.
source: The phlD mutant can be complemented for pyoluteorin production by addition of nanomolar concentrations of PG to the culture medium (Kidarsa et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Addition of nanomolar concentrations of PG induces expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes.
source: Furthermore, addition of nanomolar concentrations of PG induces expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes (Clifford et al., 2016), indicating that the influence of PG on pyoluteorin production is mediated through gene regulation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The influence of PG on pyoluteorin production is mediated through gene regulation.
source: Furthermore, addition of nanomolar concentrations of PG induces expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes (Clifford et al., 2016), indicating that the influence of PG on pyoluteorin production is mediated through gene regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that PG induces gene expression.

claim: Pyoluteorin induces expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes.
source: Pyoluteorin itself also induces expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes (Brodhagen et al., 2004; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes are expressed under the positive control of PltR.
source: The pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes are expressed under the positive control of PltR (Brodhagen et al., 2004) (Figure 1), a transcriptional regulator belonging to the LysR family.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: PltR is a transcriptional regulator belonging to the LysR family.
source: The pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes are expressed under the positive control of PltR (Brodhagen et al., 2004) (Figure 1), a transcriptional regulator belonging to the LysR family.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the protein family.

claim: Both PG and pyoluteorin are known to induce PltR-mediated transcription of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes.
source: Both PG and pyoluteorin are known to induce PltR-mediated transcription of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes, but the relative importance of the two small molecules in inducing gene expression has not been evaluated.
evidence: This statement is based on previous literature and sets up the research question.

claim: The metabolic co-regulation between DAPG and PLT biosynthetic pathways differs from known examples of metabolic co-regulation between secondary metabolic pathways.
source: The metabolic co-regulation between DAPG and PLT biosynthetic pathways differs from known examples of metabolic co-regulation between secondary metabolic pathways, which can be classified into four types based on the underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with known mechanisms described in the literature.

claim: The first type of co-regulation involves one or more intermediates that are shared by different biosynthetic pathways.
source: The first type of co-regulation involves one or more intermediates that are shared by different biosynthetic pathways (Vingadassalon et al., 2015; Cano-Prieto et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The second type of co-regulation results when a single enzyme is shared by different pathways.
source: The second type results when a single enzyme is shared by different pathways (Lazos et al., 2010; Tsunematsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The third type of co-regulation is mediated through functionally redundant enzymes present in different pathways.
source: The third type of co-regulation is mediated through functionally redundant enzymes present in different pathways (Lautru et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The fourth type of co-regulation occurs when the biosynthetic genes for two pathways are controlled by the same 'pathway-specific' regulator.
source: The fourth type occurs when the biosynthetic genes for two pathways are controlled by the same 'pathway-specific' regulator (Pérez-Llarena et al., 1997; Bergmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The DAPG and pyoluteorin pathways do not share a biosynthetic intermediate, enzymatic activity, or regulator.
source: Overall these mechanisms of metabolic co-regulation involve a shared biosynthetic intermediate, enzymatic activity, or regulator, but none of these features is shared by the DAPG and pyoluteorin pathways (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by the pathway diagrams in Figure 1 and the analysis of the gene clusters.

claim: PG is transformed by a halogenase encoded in the pyoluteorin gene cluster into chlorinated derivatives that function as cell-cell communication signals inducing expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes.
source: Our results show that PG, an intermediate in DAPG biosynthesis, is transformed by a halogenase encoded in the pyoluteorin gene cluster into chlorinated derivatives that function as cell-cell communication signals inducing expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches including genetic, biochemical, and analytical chemistry data.

claim: This work reveals a new mechanism of co-regulation between two secondary metabolic pathways, which is mediated by an intermediate in one pathway that is converted into signals that activate the second pathway.
source: Our work reveals a new mechanism of co-regulation between two secondary metabolic pathways, which is mediated by an intermediate in one pathway that is converted into signals that activate the second pathway.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the experimental findings.

claim: In the ΔpltAΔphlD double mutant grown in non-amended medium, GFP expression was significantly lower than in wild-type Pf-5 (p=2.76E-4).
source: In the non-amended medium, and relative to wild-type Pf-5, GFP expression was significantly lower in the ΔpltAΔphlD mutant (p=2.76E-4), indicating only background expression of pltL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the medium amended with 10 nM PG, GFP expression of the ΔpltAΔphlD mutant increased nearly tenfold relative to expression levels in non-amended medium.
source: In the medium amended with 10 nM PG, GFP expression of the ΔpltAΔphlD mutant increased nearly tenfold relative to expression levels in non-amended medium, indicating induction of pltL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Addition of 100 nM pyoluteorin failed to alter GFP expression by the ΔpltAΔphlD mutant.
source: In contrast, addition of 100 nM pyoluteorin failed to alter GFP expression by the ΔpltAΔphlD mutant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When both pyoluteorin and PG were added, the GFP expression was significantly higher than under treatment with PG alone (p=1.44E-4).
source: However, when both pyoluteorin and PG were added, the GFP expression was significantly higher than under treatment with PG alone (p=1.44E-4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pyoluteorin was not required for pltL expression but further induced pltL expression in the presence of PG.
source: Therefore, pyoluteorin was not required for pltL expression but further induced pltL expression in the presence of PG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: pltR is required for expression of pltL.
source: As expected based on the necessity of PltR for expression of the pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes (Brodhagen et al., 2004; Li et al., 2012), pltR was required for expression of pltL and the presence of PG could not restore pltL expression in a ΔpltAΔphlDΔpltR mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of PG could not restore pltL expression in a ΔpltAΔphlDΔpltR mutant.
source: As expected based on the necessity of PltR for expression of the pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes (Brodhagen et al., 2004; Li et al., 2012), pltR was required for expression of pltL and the presence of PG could not restore pltL expression in a ΔpltAΔphlDΔpltR mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PG, not pyoluteorin, is required for PltR-mediated activation of pltL.
source: These results indicated that PG, not pyoluteorin, is required for PltR-mediated activation of pltL.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PG failed to induce GFP expression from pRL-gfp in P. fluorescens SBW25.
source: Although PG was sufficient to induce pltL expression in Pf-5 (Figure 2), PG failed to induce GFP expression from pRL-gfp in P. fluorescens SBW25 (Figure 3A) and is therefore not likely to function as a signal directly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PG is not likely to function as a signal directly.
source: Although PG was sufficient to induce pltL expression in Pf-5 (Figure 2), PG failed to induce GFP expression from pRL-gfp in P. fluorescens SBW25 (Figure 3A) and is therefore not likely to function as a signal directly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that PG does not induce expression in SBW25.

claim: Culture supernatants from Pf-5, but not the ΔphlD mutant, could induce GFP expression of SBW25.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, culture supernatants from Pf-5, but not the ΔphlD mutant, could induce GFP expression of SBW25 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PG could be converted to a compound(s) that regulates pyoluteorin gene expression.
source: Therefore, we concluded that PG does not directly influence pyoluteorin gene expression. Rather, PG could be converted to a compound(s) that regulates pyoluteorin gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that culture supernatants from Pf-5 induce expression in SBW25.

claim: pltM is required for pyoluteorin production.
source: PltM is a putative FADH2-dependent halogenase and is required for pyoluteorin production: a pltM insertion mutant is deficient in the production of pyoluteorin (Nowak-Thompson et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and confirmed by the authors' own data.

claim: The ΔpltM mutant does not produce pyoluteorin.
source: To avoid any concerns regarding potential polar effects of the insertion in the previously derived pltM mutant (Nowak-Thompson et al., 1999), we generated a mutant with an in-frame deletion of pltM and confirmed that the ΔpltM mutant does not produce pyoluteorin (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pyoluteorin production by the ΔpltM mutant could be complemented by a plasmid-borne copy of pltM.
source: Pyoluteorin production by the ΔpltM mutant could be complemented by a plasmid-borne copy of pltM, confirming that pltM has an essential role in pyoluteorin production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ΔpltM mutant expressed only background levels of GFP, indicating that expression of pltL was not induced in this mutant.
source: We introduced pL-gfp into the ΔpltM mutant and found that the mutant expressed only background levels of GFP, indicating that expression of pltL was not induced in this mutant (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GFP expression of the ΔpltM mutant remained at background levels even when cells were grown in the presence of 10 nM PG.
source: The GFP expression remained at background levels even when cells were grown in the presence of 10 nM PG.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GFP expression of the ΔpltM mutant was induced by culture supernatants of Pf-5.
source: However, GFP expression of the ΔpltM mutant was induced by culture supernatants of Pf-5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Culture supernatants of the ΔphlD mutant failed to induce GFP expression of the ΔpltM mutant containing pL-gfp.
source: As expected, culture supernatants of the ΔphlD mutant failed to induce GFP expression of the ΔpltM mutant containing pL-gfp.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Wild-type Pf-5, but not the ΔpltM mutant, produces the compound(s) that induces the pltL expression.
source: These results supported our hypothesis and indicated that wild-type Pf-5, but not the ΔpltM mutant, produces the compound(s) that induces the pltL expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PG induced GFP expression of SBW25 containing pMRL-gfp.
source: While PG failed to induce GFP expression of SBW25 containing pRL-gfp (Figure 3A), it induced GFP expression of SBW25 containing pMRL-gfp (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: pltM is sufficient for signaling in SBW25 in the presence of PG and the regulatory gene pltR.
source: These results indicated that pltM is sufficient for signaling in SBW25 in the presence of PG and the regulatory gene pltR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 2-chlorobenzene-1,3,5-triol (PG-Cl) was present in culture extracts of the wild-type Pf-5 but not the ΔpltM mutant.
source: This analysis revealed the presence of 2-chlorobenzene-1,3,5-triol (PG-Cl) in culture extracts of the wild-type Pf-5 but not the ΔpltM mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by LCMS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two peaks in the extract of wild-type Pf-5 induced pltL expression in SBW25 (pPL-gfp).
source: We also separated the extracts of the wild-type into fractions using semi-preparatory HPLC, and assayed the fractions for signaling activity. This analysis revealed two peaks that induced pltL expression in SBW25 (pPL-gfp) (Figure 4C), suggesting that Pf-5 produces at least two signaling compounds.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Pf-5 produces at least two signaling compounds.
source: We also separated the extracts of the wild-type into fractions using semi-preparatory HPLC, and assayed the fractions for signaling activity. This analysis revealed two peaks that induced pltL expression in SBW25 (pPL-gfp) (Figure 4C), suggesting that Pf-5 produces at least two signaling compounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of two peaks with signaling activity.

claim: The identities of PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 partially purified from the culture extracts were confirmed by comparing them with the synthesized authentic compounds.
source: The identities of PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 partially purified from the culture extracts were confirmed by comparing them with the synthesized authentic compounds (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by LCMS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PG-Cl has been isolated from the red alga Rhabdoina verticillata.
source: PG-Cl, a molecule with previously undescribed biological activity, has been isolated from the red alga Rhabdoina verticillata (Blackman and Matthews, 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PG-Cl2 has not been previously reported.
source: To our knowledge, PG-Cl2 has not been previously reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the compound based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The structures of PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 are consistent with the expected products of a reaction catalyzed by PltM, an FADH2-dependent halogenase.
source: The structures of these two chlorinated phloroglucinol derivatives are consistent with the expected products of a reaction catalyzed by PltM, an FADH2-dependent halogenase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known enzymatic activity of FADH2-dependent halogenases.

claim: In the presence of co-factors and flavin reductase, PltM converted PG into a compound(s) that activated pltL expression.
source: The results showed that, in the presence of co-factors and flavin reductase, PltM converted PG into a compound(s) that activated pltL expression, as determined from GFP expression of SBW25 containing pRL-gfp (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro enzyme assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 were present in the in vitro reaction containing PltM, but not in the reaction without PltM.
source: Furthermore, LCMS analysis showed that both PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 were present in the in vitro reaction containing PltM, but not in the reaction without PltM, based on comparisons with the authentic standards (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by LCMS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PltM exhibits a high degree of substrate specificity.
source: By evaluating a range of compounds related to PG as possible precursors, we also demonstrated that PltM exhibits a high degree of substrate specificity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: pltM is necessary and sufficient for converting PG into PG-Cl and PG-Cl2, which induce pltL expression.
source: These in vitro data, combined with the genetic data above, demonstrate that pltM is necessary and sufficient for converting PG into PG-Cl and PG-Cl2, which induce pltL expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Addition of synthesized PG-Cl or PG-Cl2 to cultures induced, in a concentration-dependent manner, expression of pltL by the ΔpltM mutant of Pf-5.
source: Addition of synthesized PG-Cl or PG-Cl2 to cultures induced, in a concentration-dependent manner, expression of pltL (Figure 6A and B) and pyoluteorin production (Figure 6C and D) by the ΔpltM mutant of Pf-5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Addition of synthesized PG-Cl or PG-Cl2 to cultures induced, in a concentration-dependent manner, pyoluteorin production by the ΔpltM mutant of Pf-5.
source: Addition of synthesized PG-Cl or PG-Cl2 to cultures induced, in a concentration-dependent manner, expression of pltL (Figure 6A and B) and pyoluteorin production (Figure 6C and D) by the ΔpltM mutant of Pf-5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The minimum concentration of PG-Cl2 that induced the expression of pltL or production of pyoluteorin was 0.01 μM, which is 100-fold less than that observed for PG-Cl.
source: The minimum concentration of PG-Cl2 that induced the expression of pltL or production of pyoluteorin was 0.01 μM, which is 100-fold less than that observed for PG-Cl.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: PG-Cl2 is a more potent signaling compound than PG-Cl.
source: These results suggest that PG-Cl2 is a more potent signaling compound than PG-Cl.
evidence: This is an inference based on the concentration-response data.

claim: Above 0.1 µM PG-Cl2, growth of P. protegens Pf-5 decreased.
source: Additionally, there is evidence of toxicity: above 0.1 µM PG-Cl2, growth of P. protegens Pf-5 decreased (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PG-Cl was toxic to Pf-5, but only at concentrations of 10 μM or higher.
source: PG-Cl was also toxic to Pf-5, but only at concentrations of 10 μM or higher.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 showed inhibitory effects on the growth of P. fluorescens strain SBW25.
source: Similarly, PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 showed inhibitory effects on the growth of P. fluorescens strain SBW25 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Induction of pltL expression and pyoluteorin production by both PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 required pltR.
source: Induction of pltL expression and pyoluteorin production by both PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 required pltR (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 induced pyoluteorin production concurrently with decreased monoacetylphloroglucinol (MAPG) and DAPG production by the ΔpltM mutant.
source: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 induced pyoluteorin production concurrently with decreased monoacetylphloroglucinol (MAPG) and DAPG production by the ΔpltM mutant (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: This result is consistent with the known co-regulation between the pyoluteorin and DAPG biosynthetic pathways.
source: This result is consistent with the known co-regulation between the pyoluteorin and DAPG biosynthetic pathways (Brodhagen et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement connects the current findings to previous literature.

claim: DAPG and pyoluteorin are known signals produced by distinct biosynthetic pathways with described roles in intercellular communication of P. protegens.
source: DAPG and pyoluteorin are known signals produced by distinct biosynthetic pathways with described roles in intercellular communication of P. protegens (Schnider-Keel et al., 2000; Brodhagen et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 are released by the bacterial cell.
source: Several observations suggested that PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 also function as cell-cell communication signals: (1) they are released by the bacterial cell (Figure 3 and Figure 4);
evidence: This is supported by the detection of these compounds in culture supernatants.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 can be taken up by the bacterial cell.
source: Several observations suggested that PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 also function as cell-cell communication signals: (1) they are released by the bacterial cell (Figure 3 and Figure 4); (2) they can be taken up by the bacterial cell (Figure 6);
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that exogenously added compounds induce gene expression.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 regulate gene expression at the transcriptional level and affect the output (antibiotic production) of the cell.
source: Several observations suggested that PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 also function as cell-cell communication signals: (1) they are released by the bacterial cell (Figure 3 and Figure 4); (2) they can be taken up by the bacterial cell (Figure 6); (3) they regulate gene expression at the transcriptional level and affect the output (antibiotic production) of the cell (Figure 6);
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing induction of gene expression and antibiotic production.

claim: Production of PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 varies with the growth stage of the bacterial cultures.
source: Several observations suggested that PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 also function as cell-cell communication signals: (1) they are released by the bacterial cell (Figure 3 and Figure 4); (2) they can be taken up by the bacterial cell (Figure 6); (3) they regulate gene expression at the transcriptional level and affect the output (antibiotic production) of the cell (Figure 6); (4) their production varies with the growth stage of the bacterial cultures (Figure 7—figure supplement 1);
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The regulatory activities of PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 rely on a transcriptional regulator, PltR.
source: Several observations suggested that PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 also function as cell-cell communication signals: (1) they are released by the bacterial cell (Figure 3 and Figure 4); (2) they can be taken up by the bacterial cell (Figure 6); (3) they regulate gene expression at the transcriptional level and affect the output (antibiotic production) of the cell (Figure 6); (4) their production varies with the growth stage of the bacterial cultures (Figure 7—figure supplement 1); and (5) their regulatory activities rely on a transcriptional regulator, PltR (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: PG can function as a chemical messenger between cells of P. protegens.
source: These results, combined with our previous finding that PG can function as a chemical messenger between cells of P. protegens (Clifford et al., 2016), collectively support the model depicted in Figure 7A, in which PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 can be synthesized from PG by bacterial cells, released into the environment and taken up by neighboring cells to induce expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes and produce pyoluteorin.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pyoluteorin was produced when the ΔphlAΔpltM and ΔphlAΔphlDΔpltA mutants were grown in co-culture.
source: Neither mutant could produce pyoluteorin when grown in pure culture, because of the phlD and pltA mutations in the ΔphlAΔphlDΔpltA mutant and the pltM mutation in the ΔphlAΔpltM mutant. In contrast, pyoluteorin was produced when the two mutants were grown in co-culture (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Both ΔphlAΔpltM and ΔphlAΔphlDΔpltA mutants showed increased expression of pltL in the co-culture compared with the mutants grown in pure culture.
source: Consistently, both mutants showed increased expression of pltL in the co-culture compared with the mutants grown in pure culture (Table 1, Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 7B.

claim: PG produced by the ΔphlAΔpltM mutant could be converted into PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 by co-cultured cells of the ΔphlAΔphlDΔpltA mutant.
source: These results support our model (Figure 7A) that PG produced by the ΔphlAΔpltM mutant could be converted into PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 by co-cultured cells of the ΔphlAΔphlDΔpltA mutant; PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 could then be used by the ΔphlAΔpltM mutant to induce production of pyoluteorin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-culture experimental data.

claim: The co-culture, but not the pure cultures, of the ΔphlAΔpltM and ΔphlAΔphlDΔpltA mutants inhibited the growth of E. amylovora.
source: As expected, the co-culture, but not the pure cultures, of the two mutants inhibited the growth of E. amylovora (Figure 7C), a plant pathogenic bacterium that is sensitive to pyoluteorin (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: E. amylovora is sensitive to pyoluteorin.
source: As expected, the co-culture, but not the pure cultures, of the two mutants inhibited the growth of E. amylovora (Figure 7C), a plant pathogenic bacterium that is sensitive to pyoluteorin (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The primary contribution of this work was the discovery of a novel mechanism of co-regulation between secondary metabolite biosynthetic pathways.
source: The primary contribution of this work was the discovery of a novel mechanism of co-regulation between secondary metabolite biosynthetic pathways (Figure 8).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: This co-regulatory mechanism involves a metabolic intermediate that is transformed through enzymatic activity into a signal regulating gene expression.
source: This co-regulatory mechanism involves a metabolic intermediate that is transformed through enzymatic activity into a signal regulating gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism discovered in the study.

claim: The metabolic intermediate responsible for coordination of DAPG and pyoluteorin production is not shared by the two biosynthetic pathways.
source: In contrast to previously described co-regulatory mechanisms involving a metabolic intermediate (Vingadassalon et al., 2015; Cano-Prieto et al., 2015), the metabolic intermediate responsible for coordination of DAPG and pyoluteorin production is not shared by the two biosynthetic pathways.
evidence: This distinguishes the current mechanism from previously described mechanisms.

claim: PG is an intermediate in DAPG biosynthesis and a precursor for formation of signaling molecules that activate expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes.
source: Instead, PG is an intermediate in DAPG biosynthesis and a precursor for formation of signaling molecules that activate expression of pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes (Figure 8).
evidence: This is the key finding of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The role of antibiotics in cell-cell signaling is now widely recognized.
source: The role of antibiotics in cell-cell signaling is now widely recognized (Yim et al., 2007), but the results of this study show that intermediates of antibiotic biosynthesis pathways can also function as, or be converted to, signaling molecules.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Intermediates of antibiotic biosynthesis pathways can also function as, or be converted to, signaling molecules.
source: The role of antibiotics in cell-cell signaling is now widely recognized (Yim et al., 2007), but the results of this study show that intermediates of antibiotic biosynthesis pathways can also function as, or be converted to, signaling molecules.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: The final products DAPG and pyoluteorin, the biosynthetic intermediate PG, and its derivatives PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 all serve as signals influencing gene expression, the production of antibiotics, and the antimicrobial activity of P. protegens.
source: Therefore, it appears that the final products DAPG and pyoluteorin, the biosynthetic intermediate PG, and its derivatives PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 all serve as signals influencing gene expression, the production of antibiotics, and the antimicrobial activity of P. protegens (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings from the current study and previous literature.

claim: The signaling roles of small molecules released as intermediates, derivatives, or end products of antibiotic biosynthesis pathways are likely to be more consequential than previously recognized.
source: The signaling roles of small molecules released as intermediates, derivatives, or end products of antibiotic biosynthesis pathways are likely to be more consequential than previously recognized.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: LysR regulators typically require a signal for activity, and the signal is commonly an intermediate or product of the regulated gene cluster.
source: LysR regulators typically require a signal for activity, and the signal is commonly an intermediate or product of the regulated gene cluster (Maddocks and Oyston, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Pyoluteorin has been proposed to be the signal of PltR.
source: Pyoluteorin has been proposed to be the signal of PltR (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The signaling effect of pyoluteorin relies on the presence of PG.
source: However, our data indicate that the signaling effect of pyoluteorin relies on the presence of PG (Figure 2), which is converted to PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 (Figure 3 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2, rather than pyoluteorin, are signals required for the activity of PltR.
source: Nevertheless, based on our data that PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 are required for induction of the pyoluteorin biosynthetic genes (Figure 6), and pltR is required for the signaling action of PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 in both P. protegens Pf-5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) and P. fluorescens SBW25 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), we speculate that that PG-Cl and PG-Cl2, rather than pyoluteorin, are signals required for the activity of PltR.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: P. protegens can occupy different environments, including the soil, plant surfaces, and insects.
source: P. protegens can occupy different environments, including the soil, plant surfaces, and insects, and interact with different organisms including bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and insects (Brodhagen et al., 2004; Jousset et al., 2009; Kidarsa et al., 2013; Henkels et al., 2014; Loper et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both DAPG and pyoluteorin contribute to the antagonism of P. protegens against a range of bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes.
source: Both DAPG and pyoluteorin contribute to the antagonism of P. protegens against a range of bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes (Ohmori et al., 1978; Keel et al., 1992) and both facilitate the bacterium's establishment in fungal tissues, such as basidiocarps of the button mushroom Agaricus spp. (Henkels et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both DAPG and pyoluteorin facilitate the bacterium's establishment in fungal tissues, such as basidiocarps of the button mushroom Agaricus spp.
source: Both DAPG and pyoluteorin contribute to the antagonism of P. protegens against a range of bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes (Ohmori et al., 1978; Keel et al., 1992) and both facilitate the bacterium's establishment in fungal tissues, such as basidiocarps of the button mushroom Agaricus spp. (Henkels et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The sensitivity of a specific organism to DAPG and pyoluteorin can be different.
source: However, the sensitivity of a specific organism to these two antibiotics can be different. For example, pyoluteorin is twenty times more toxic than DAPG to the growth of E. amylovora (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pyoluteorin is twenty times more toxic than DAPG to the growth of E. amylovora.
source: For example, pyoluteorin is twenty times more toxic than DAPG to the growth of E. amylovora (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: DAPG but not pyoluteorin exhibits toxicity to the amoeba Acanthamoeba castellanii.
source: For example, DAPG but not pyoluteorin exhibits toxicity to the amoeba Acanthamoeba castellanii (Jousset and Bonkowski, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Natural situations may exist in which it could be more advantageous to produce one compound versus the other.
source: Therefore, natural situations may exist in which it could be more advantageous to produce one compound versus the other.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential activities of the two antibiotics.

claim: Antibiotic biosynthesis is associated with metabolic costs.
source: Additionally, antibiotic biosynthesis is associated with metabolic costs.
evidence: This is general knowledge about secondary metabolism.

claim: The coordinated production of pyoluteorin and DAPG may be a mechanism for the bacterium to balance metabolic cost against the benefits conferred by production of the two antibiotics.
source: The coordinated production of pyoluteorin and DAPG may be a mechanism for the bacterium to balance metabolic cost against the benefits conferred by production of the two antibiotics.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary significance of the co-regulation.

claim: Metabolic co-regulation may enable bacteria to activate the production of one antibiotic to combat certain competitors or predators or to occupy specific habitats, while reducing the metabolic burden on the cell by repressing the production of a second compound.
source: In short, metabolic co-regulation may enable bacteria to activate the production of one antibiotic to combat certain competitors or predators or to occupy specific habitats, while reducing the metabolic burden on the cell by repressing the production of a second compound.
evidence: This is a speculation about the ecological significance of the co-regulation.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 are now known to be responsible for the previously described activation of the pyoluteorin biosynthesis by nanomolar concentrations of PG.
source: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 are now known to be responsible for the previously described activation of the pyoluteorin biosynthesis by nanomolar concentrations of PG, but these compounds do not appear to mediate the repression of pyoluteorin production by higher (micromolar) concentrations of PG (Kidarsa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 do not appear to mediate the repression of pyoluteorin production by higher (micromolar) concentrations of PG.
source: PG-Cl and PG-Cl2 are now known to be responsible for the previously described activation of the pyoluteorin biosynthesis by nanomolar concentrations of PG, but these compounds do not appear to mediate the repression of pyoluteorin production by higher (micromolar) concentrations of PG (Kidarsa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the chlorinated compounds induce rather than repress pyoluteorin production.

claim: The mechanism(s) involved in inhibition of pyoluteorin production by PG remain unknown.
source: The mechanism(s) involved in inhibition of pyoluteorin production by PG remain unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in understanding.

claim: This study reports a novel mechanism of co-regulation that is responsible for only one aspect of the complex and intricate co-regulation of two secondary metabolites in P. protegens.
source: Here, we report a novel mechanism of co-regulation that is responsible for only one aspect of the complex and intricate co-regulation of two secondary metabolites in P. protegens.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the scope of the findings.

claim: The results highlight the diversity of mechanisms involved in metabolic co-regulation in bacteria.
source: Our results highlight the diversity of mechanisms involved in metabolic co-regulation in bacteria and provide an unprecedented example of co-regulation between separate biosynthetic pathways in which the intermediate of one pathway functions as a precursor of the signal(s) activating the biosynthesis of a second pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader significance of the findings.

claim: This study provides an unprecedented example of co-regulation between separate biosynthetic pathways in which the intermediate of one pathway functions as a precursor of the signal(s) activating the biosynthesis of a second pathway.
